🌱 PTMC Jr. Final Project Report 
Team Name: The Renaissance 
Team Members: Harlem Phipps, Sydney Brooks, Avery Brooks 
Challenge Division: Middle School 
Optimizing Lunar Regolith for Purple Radish Microgreen Growth 
Using Nutrient and Drainage System Design 
🎥 Video Documentation / YouTube Links 
Section

Background 
Our team chose the Plant the Moon Challenge because future Artemis missions will require 
astronauts to grow food in environments where normal Earth soil is not available. We wanted to 
investigate whether lunar regolith simulant could be improved enough to support fast, 
nutrient-dense crops that might help feed astronauts on the Moon. 
We selected Purple Radish microgreens because they grow quickly in about 7–8 days, are 
nutrient-dense, and can produce harvests in a short time. We also wanted to explore whether 
microgreens could serve as the first stage of a multi-stage lunar growing system, where some 
plants are harvested early for nutrition, some are grown to maturity for food, and some are 
grown to the seed-producing stage for future planting. 
1

📷Team photo 
 
 📷 Purple radish seed packet + mediums 
 
 
 
Experimental Rationale 
This experiment brings value to the scientific community because it explores not only whether 
plants can grow in lunar regolith simulant, but how the regolith can be engineered to grow 
better. Rather than stopping at a simple comparison between Burpee potting mix and lunar 
regolith, our team tested how drainage design, moisture management, and hydroponic nutrients 
could improve crop performance. 
Our project also contributes to space agriculture research by showing that the most important 
challenge may not be just “soil quality,” but how water and nutrients are delivered during 
different plant growth stages, especially during germination. 
📷Side-by-side photo of Burpee trays (green) and lunar regolith trays (blue) 
2

Hypothesis 
If lunar regolith simulant is improved with MaxiGro hydroponic nutrients and a drainage system 
that keeps the seed layer moist but not oversaturated, then Purple Radish microgreens will grow 
better than in untreated lunar regolith and may grow nearly as well as or better than those 
grown in Burpee Natural & Organic Potting Mix, which served as the Earth-based control 
growing medium. 
Independent Variable 
The independent variable was the growing system used with the lunar regolith simulant, 
including: 
●​ untreated lunar regolith 
●​ regolith with MaxiGro hydroponic nutrient solution 
●​ regolith with two different drainage system designs 
●​ regolith with an optimized root-zone moisture system 
For comparison, Burpee Natural & Organic Potting Mix served as the Earth-based control 
growing medium. 
Dependent Variables 
The dependent variables measured were: 
●​ germination success 
●​ survival rate 
●​ harvest yield (mL of harvested microgreens) 
●​ visible growth speed 
●​ overall plant health and vigor 
Time-lapse videos and photos were also used to compare: 
●​ speed of germination 
3

●​ growth progression 
●​ tray consistency 
●​ and visible root-zone performance 
Controls / Constants 
The following variables were kept as consistent as possible across all rounds: 
●​ same seed type: Purple Radish 
●​ same seed amount: 1/2 tablespoon per tray 
●​ same amount of growing medium: 3/4 cup per tray 
●​ same tray size and tray style 
●​ same light source 
●​ same general grow location 
●​ same approximate grow period (7–8 days) 
●​ same harvesting method 
●​ same documentation methods (photos, video, timelapse) 
Tray Color Coding 
●​ Green trays = Burpee Natural & Organic Potting Mix control 
●​ Blue trays = Lunar regolith simulant 
Grow Pot Setup 
Each tray contained: 
●​ 3/4 cup of growing medium 
●​ 1/2 tablespoon of Purple Radish seeds 
Burpee Control Trays (Green) 
Contained: 
●​ Burpee Natural & Organic Potting Mix only 
Lunar Regolith Trays (Blue) 
Contained: 
●​ lunar regolith simulant 
●​ later rounds also included: 
4

○​ MaxiGro hydroponic nutrient solution 
○​ mesh screen barriers 
○​ pea gravel drainage layers 
○​ lower liquid reservoir system 
Drainage Design 1 
●​ mesh screen and pea gravel placed inside the upper tray beneath the regolith 
Drainage Design 2 
●​ mesh screen placed at the bottom of the upper tray 
●​ pea gravel placed in a second tray underneath 
●​ lower tray acted as a nutrient/moisture reservoir 
●​ roots could grow downward toward liquid while seeds stayed less saturated 
📷 Drainage Design 1 and 2 
 
 
MaxiGro Nutrient Solution Preparation 
In Rounds 2 and 3, our team prepared a MaxiGro hydroponic nutrient solution using 1 
tablespoon per 1 gallon of water. This provided essential nutrients that lunar regolith does not 
contain, such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. 
5

The solution was applied by pouring it into the lower reservoir and lightly spraying the surface to 
support germination. This allowed roots to grow downward toward nutrients while keeping seeds 
moist. 
Plants grown with MaxiGro showed stronger roots, faster growth, and higher yields than 
those grown with water alone, especially when combined with our drainage system, which 
prevented oversaturation and improved nutrient access. 
📷 Maxi Grow Solution 
 
Procedures 
The experiment was conducted in three rounds. 
Round 1 – Baseline Comparison 
The team compared: 
●​ Burpee Natural & Organic Potting Mix 
●​ untreated lunar regolith simulant 
Each tray received: 
●​ approximately 1/2 cup of water 
This round was used to observe baseline differences in survival, growth, and moisture behavior. 
Round 2 – Drainage System Comparison 
The team tested four lunar regolith trays using: 
●​ MaxiGro hydroponic nutrient solution 
●​ two different drainage system designs 
Setup: 
6

●​ 2 trays used Drainage Design 1 
●​ 2 trays used Drainage Design 2 
For lunar regolith trays: 
●​ approximately 1/2 cup of MaxiGro solution 
●​ plus 4 top sprays per tray to keep the seed zone moist 
This round tested whether the position of the water relative to the seeds and roots affected 
growth. 
Round 3 – Optimized System 
In Round 3, all four lunar regolith trays used: 
●​ lunar regolith simulant 
●​ MaxiGro nutrient solution 
●​ Drainage Design 2 (the strongest-performing design from Round 2) 
For each lunar regolith tray: 
●​ approximately 1/2 cup of MaxiGro solution 
●​ plus 4 top sprays per tray 
This round tested whether the strongest-performing design from Round 2 would produce more 
repeatable results. 
Watering / Moisture Management Protocol 
Watering was adjusted based on the moisture behavior of each growing medium. 
Burpee Natural & Organic Potting Mix 
The Burpee control trays generally required watering approximately once every 2–3 days, using 
about 100 mL per tray. The Burpee potting mix absorbed water effectively and released 
moisture more slowly over time. 
Lunar Regolith Simulant 
The lunar regolith trays generally required daily moisture support, averaging approximately 40 
mL per day or equivalent moisture support through the lower reservoir system and top sprays. 
The regolith dried out more quickly at the surface and required more frequent moisture 
management. 
7

Important Moisture Observation 
In Round 2, two lunar regolith trays performed poorly because the seeds sat too directly in 
pooled MaxiGro solution. This suggested that Purple Radish seeds performed best when kept 
moist, but not submerged. 
📷 Photo showing a pooled liquid problem in the failed Round 2 tray

Data was collected using: 
●​ tray-by-tray harvest yield (mL) 
●​ survival counts 
●​ visual growth observations 
●​ germination timing observations 
●​ photo documentation 
●​ 8-day timelapse videos for each round 
Each timelapse covered approximately: 
●​ 8 total days 
●​ including 2–3 days of germination 
The team also used: 
●​ a Wyze security camera placed at Harlem’s house 
●​ the Wyze app for remote observation 
●​ weekly Google Meet check-ins for collaborative monitoring and experiment review 
Because the experiment was conducted at Harlem’s house, Sydney and Avery participated by: 
8

●​ monitoring trays through the camera app 
●​ attending weekly Google Meet meetings 
●​ coming in person for major plantings and harvests 
This allowed the team to work collaboratively even when not all members were physically 
present.

Key Quantitative Findings 
●​ Round 1 lunar regolith yield: 63 mL 
●​ Round 3 lunar regolith yield: 264 mL 
●​ Total lunar regolith yield improvement: +201 mL 
●​ Overall increase from Round 1 to Round 3: 319% 
Comparison to Burpee Control 
10

●​ Round 1: lunar regolith achieved 25% of Burpee control yield 
●​ Round 2: lunar regolith achieved 60.3% of Burpee control yield 
●​ Round 3: lunar regolith achieved 86.0% of Burpee control yield 
Timelapse Observation 
The lunar regolith trays generally germinated 12–36 hours slower than the Burpee control 
trays. However, in healthy trays, growth accelerated after roots extended downward into the 
MaxiGro nutrient reservoir. 
📷Round 1 harvest photo: Burpee vs lunar 
 
 
📷Round 2 side-by-side comparison: Design 1 vs Design 2 
 
 
📷 Round 3 tray comparison 
 
11

📷Harvest measuring / weighing photo 
 
 
Analysis 
Our data showed that lunar regolith improved a lot over time. In Round 1, it only produced 63 
mL compared to 252 mL in the Burpee soil, and only about 25% of the trays did well. By Round 
3, it produced 264 mL, which was about 86% of the Burpee yield—a huge 319% improvement. 
This showed that regolith isn’t just “bad soil.” The real problem was how water and nutrients 
were delivered, especially at the beginning. 
From our timelapse videos, we saw two clear growth phases. During germination, regolith was 
slower by about 12–36 hours, which made early growth harder. But once roots reached the 
nutrient reservoir, growth sped up a lot—and some trays even caught up to the Burpee soil. 
The best system kept seeds moist (not soaked), separated them from standing water, and let 
roots grow down into nutrients. This means growing plants on the Moon might depend more on 
how we design the system than the regolith itself. 
📷 Root photo showing roots reaching downward into the reservoir 
 
12

Conclusions 
Our hypothesis was supported. When we improved the lunar regolith with MaxiGro nutrients and 
a better drainage system, the plants grew much better. By the final round, the regolith trays 
produced 264 mL compared to 307 mL in the Burpee soil, reaching about 86% of the control. 
One of the coolest things we discovered was that regolith didn’t work well at first—but got much 
better once the roots reached the nutrient reservoir. This shows that plants on the Moon might 
need different systems for early growth versus later growth. 
Overall, we learned that growing food in lunar regolith is possible—but only if the system is 
carefully designed to control moisture, drainage, and nutrients. 
 
Future Considerations 
If we repeated this experiment, we would improve it by: 
●​ measuring germination timing more precisely 
●​ measuring root length 
●​ testing different spray amounts during the first 72 hours 
●​ testing different depths of pea gravel 
●​ testing different nutrient concentrations 
●​ testing separate systems for germination vs later growth 
We also want to continue exploring our multi-stage lunar food system idea: 
1.​ harvest some plants early as microgreens 
2.​ grow some into full edible plants 
3.​ grow some to the seed-producing stage for future crops 
We began exploring this by attempting to grow some harvested microgreens into full plants. 
Although that test was not successful because of under-watering, we believe this could become 
a promising next step in building a more sustainable lunar growing system.
